newsitem.title: USA: Gov. Dean tries to lure mutual funds to Vermont.
newsitem.headline: Gov. Dean tries to lure mutual funds to Vermont.

text.p: Vermont Gov. Howard Dean made a lighting strike visit to Boston in hopes of "getting better paying jobs" and convincing financial services companies in Massachusetts to move to his state.
He said he plans a similar trip to New York in late April.

Dean, speaking to Boston Securities Analysts Society Thursday, said he visited five financial services firms in the city in the hope that they would move at least part of their operations to his state.

"The unemployment rate in my state is 4.4 percent. It's not more jobs that I need. I need better paying jobs," Dean told the analysts, explaining he seeks to attract financial firms, telecommunications companies and manufacturing plants, but not retail outlets.
Dean also said he expected to reach "a reasonable accommodation with the utilties" in Vermont.

Saying the utilties represented not only a great many jobs, but were for the most part all headquartered in his state, Dean said he "will try to reach an accommodation which doesn't bankrupt them and that they can live with."

Vermont's citizen legislature is debating Dean's $1.6 billion budget which includes a modest $43 million in capital spending. The legislative session is scheduled to end in April at which point, Dean said he hoped the final budget would include a rainy day fund.
He noted Vermont has emerged from the 1990 recession by passing budgets that cut spending while at the same time expanded social programs.

"I think the federal government will wind up doing what we have done in Vermont with welfare reform and I hope they will do what we have done with making sure that every child in our state under the age of 18 has medical insurance," the former internist said.

Vermont's welfare program requires that those who receive it work "and we do that by guaranteeing child care, job training and a job," he said with the result that Vermont has lowered its welfare costs by about 20 percent.

Dean also signed legislation that insures every child under the age of 18 in a family of four making $35,000 or less and he also instituted a program that offers a home visit to new parents within the first two weeks of birth.
He credits these programs with "reducing the teenage pregnancy rate by 20 percent" and cutting reports of "child physical and sexual abuse by 30 percent" in his state.
"If you have a state that has done welfare reform... you have a state that has begun to build an infrastructure for employment," Dean concluded.
